content: This guideline is designed to be applicable to various subnational jurisdictions and authorities. It advises readers to consider all policy options that could influence the pricing, affordability, and accessibility of pharmaceutical products, including those beyond the scope of this document. Examples of such policies include those related to the selection of pharmaceutical products and intellectual property management. Ensuring coherence and consistency among related policies is essential to make them mutually reinforcing and to avoid inefficiencies or unintended consequences. The guideline encourages countries to adhere to eight overarching principles outlined in Section 2, which are relevant to the planning and implementation of all pharmaceutical pricing policies. In alignment with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), the guideline urges government authorities to take concrete actions through robust pricing policies to achieve affordable access to high-quality, effective, and safe pharmaceutical and health products. Target Audience The primary audience for this guideline includes policymakers and decision-makers responsible for introducing and revising price-management policies to improve access to pharmaceutical products. Additionally, managers and personnel involved in the operational planning of procurement, distribution, and reimbursement of pharmaceuticals may find this guideline useful. It may also benefit donors, development partners, and other stakeholders assisting countries in developing their pharmaceutical sectors and ensuring the supply of medicines. The guideline is intended for use in countries of all income levels, with specific implementation needs highlighted for lowand middle-income countries, where pricing regulations may require stronger support. However, it is also relevant for high-income settings. Scope of Content The guideline addresses two key questions related to pharmaceutical pricing: 1. Which pharmaceutical pricing policies are effective in managing the prices of medicines, considering their impacts on volume, availability, and affordability? 2. What contextual factors and implementation strategies influence the effects of specific pricing policies? The guideline covers ten pricing policies that can be applied to set, manage, or influence the prices of pharmaceutical products. These include: 1. External reference pricing 2. Internal reference pricing 3. Value-based pricing 4. Mark-up regulation across the supply and distribution chain 5. Promoting price transparency 6. Tendering and negotiation 7. Pooled procurement 9. Cost-plus pricing 10. Tax exemptions or reductions for pharmaceutical products The policies were identified based on the 2015 guideline and consultations with pharmaceutical pricing experts. Four additional policies—internal reference pricing, promoting price transparency, tendering and negotiation, and pooled procurement—are included in this revised guideline. The policy on health technology assessment has been reframed as value-based pricing to reflect its broader applications beyond pricing. Method of Guideline Development The development of this guideline followed the processes outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. The process included four main steps: 1. Planning: WHO identified contributors, including a steering group, a guideline development group (GDG), and an external review group. These groups identified priority questions and outcomes, which were approved by the WHO Guideline Review Committee. 2. Evidence Appraisal: A systematic literature review was conducted by a team of researchers to critically appraise evidence related to the guideline's scope. The GRADE methodology was applied to assess the certainty of evidence. 3. Recommendations Development: The GDG formulated recommendations during a three-day meeting in Geneva in February 2020, based on evidence reports and decision tables summarizing policy importance, evidence of effects, equity, feasibility, and other factors. 4. Review and Publication: The draft guideline was reviewed by the GDG, WHO steering group, and external reviewers. After revisions, it was approved by the WHO Guideline Review Committee in August 2020. Dissemination Plan The guideline will be disseminated electronically via the WHO website, with plain-language summaries developed to reach a broader audience. A companion publication illustrating country-specific pharmaceutical pricing policies will also be created. The guideline and its derivative products will be translated into other WHO official languages as needed. Updating and User Feedback The guideline will be updated in 2025 or earlier if substantial new evidence emerges, particularly from low-income countries or areas where evidence certainty is low. Future updates will also consider user feedback on the clarity and usability of the recommendations. Principles for Pharmaceutical Pricing Policies WHO recommends that countries adhere to eight principles when formulating and implementing pharmaceutical pricing policies: 1. Clear Purpose: 2. Context Specificity: Policies should consider local health system factors, including supply and demand dynamics. 3. Policy Coherence: Pricing policies should align with other health and pharmaceutical sector policies to avoid conflicts and inefficiencies. 4. Integrated Framework: Policies should be integrated with legislative frameworks, administrative structures, and technical capacities. 5. Transparency: Processes, methods, and outcomes of pricing policies should be clearly communicated to stakeholders. 6. Monitoring and Review: 7. Compliance and Enforcement: Compliance should be encouraged through incentives, monitored with routine data, and enforced with proportional penalties. 8. Collaboration: Countries should collaborate with other health systems and stakeholders to share information and skills. External Reference Pricing External reference pricing involves using the price of a pharmaceutical product in one or more jurisdictions as a benchmark to set or negotiate prices in another jurisdiction. However, it may not guarantee affordability and requires careful selection of reference countries based on factors such as income levels and market size. WHO suggests using external reference pricing alongside other policies, ensuring adequate resources and skilled personnel for implementation. Internal Reference Pricing Internal reference pricing involves using the prices of therapeutically comparable and interchangeable products to set a benchmark price. This policy aims to harmonize prices among similar products and encourage competition. Implementation requires selecting groups of comparable products and setting reference prices based on evidence of equivalence. It is commonly used to set reimbursement rates in healthcare systems with public or regulated private pharmaceutical insurance.
